title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI systems by seeding the web with fabricated authoritative content. A shell institution with no legal existence and no physical location published a very large volume of text designed to read as academic analysis, with the explicit goal of shaping what chatbots retrieve and repeat. The failure mode is not one inside an AI model itself but in the conditions upstream of it: language models that learn from or cite web content have no reliable mechanism to verify whether a source institution actually exists.

The deployment-stage problem is that AI systems, whether during training or at inference when retrieving sources, treat surface markers of credibility, such as formal prose, report formatting, and volume of output, as proxies for legitimacy. A campaign engineered around those proxies can enter a model's knowledge or its retrieval pool without triggering any check. Catching it would have required either source-verification steps that confirmed an institution's legal and physical existence before its content was weighted, or human editorial review of sources feeding training data.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system was in fact altered in its outputs as a result of this content, or to what degree the material has already been incorporated into training datasets.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by Israel, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence systems. The institute, which has no legal entity status or physical address, presented pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including allegations of genocide and war crimes in Gaza. The New York production company Piro Inc registered the site with the US Justice Department as material distributed for the Israeli government under foreign agent disclosure requirements. The reports were crafted to appear academically rigorous while consistently framing information to blunt criticism of Israel.

The campaign represents part of a broader effort funded by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government routed through the European advertising company Havas Media to manipulate chatbot responses. Contracts show the work involved deploying websites designed specifically to generate favorable results in AI conversations. The Hanover Institute's content has not been published since reports about it emerged in August 2026, though experts warn the material may already influence AI training data. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about such public diplomacy spending, noting that despite significant investment, American public opinion toward Israel has sharply declined since 2022.
